name: The Hall of Letters
goal: Manipulate text by index, slice and method, and know why strings cannot be edited in place.

description.what: How Python lets you reach into a piece of text: one character at a time by position, a run of characters at a time by slice, and whole transformations at a time by method.
description.why: Almost everything a program receives from a person or a file arrives as text, and almost nothing useful can be done with it until it has been cut apart, cleaned up and put back together.
description.enables: You will be able to pull a character or a run of characters out of any text by position, clean and reshape it with the built-in methods, build a formatted line from values you already hold, and cut a line into its parts and rejoin them in a new form.
description.assumes: You can write a function with parameters and a return value, use a loop to build up a result, write an if statement, and call `len` on a piece of text.
description.assessed: You will predict what indexing and slicing produce, repair code that tries to change a character in place, and write functions that take text apart and rebuild it - with the later prompts telling you only what the result should be, never how to get it.

sections.title: Counting From Zero
sections.body:
A piece of text is not one lump. It is a **sequence** of characters in a fixed order, and every character has a number - its **index** - saying where in that order it sits. Square brackets written after the text ask for the character at one index, so `word[0]` is the first.

The first index is `0`, not `1`. That looks like a trap and is actually the reason the arithmetic works out: an index is a distance from the start, so the first character is zero steps in. `len(word)` counts the characters, so the last index is always `len(word) - 1` - one less than the count, for exactly the same reason.

Because reaching the last character that way is so common, Python offers a shorthand: a **negative** index counts back from the end, so `word[-1]` is the last character and `word[-2]` the one before it. There is no `word[-0]`, because `-0` is `0`.

An index that does not exist is an error, not an empty answer. Asking for `word[8]` of an eight-character word raises `IndexError: string index out of range`, and the traceback points at the line that asked.
sections.code:
word = "grimoire"
print(word[0])
print(word[3])
print(word[-1])
print(word[-2])
print(len(word))

annotations.text: Index 0 is the first character, so this prints g. Reading it as 'zero steps from the start' makes the counting stop feeling arbitrary.
-1 is the last character. It is shorthand for word[len(word) - 1], which is the same thing written the long way.
len counts characters, so the valid indexes here are 0 to 7. word[8] would raise IndexError.

checkpoint.explain: The tempting answer for the first line is `p`, from counting the first character as number one. The tempting answer for the second is `n`, from reading -3 as 'the third character'. Both come from one mistake: an index is a distance, and a negative index is a distance measured from the far end.

sections.title: Slices, and the Half-Open Interval
sections.body:
One character at a time is rarely what you want. `word[start:end]` hands back a whole run of characters as a new piece of text - a **slice**.

The rule that catches everybody: the slice **includes** `start` and **excludes** `end`. `word[0:4]` gives you characters 0, 1, 2 and 3, and stops. This is the same half-open convention `range(0, 4)` uses, and it is deliberate rather than careless. It buys two things: the length of the slice is always `end - start`, and adjacent slices join up perfectly, so `word[0:4]` followed by `word[4:8]` rebuilds the whole word with nothing dropped and nothing repeated.

Either end may be left out. `word[:4]` means from the beginning, `word[4:]` means to the end, and `word[:]` means the whole thing. Negative numbers work here too, so `word[-3:]` is the last three characters.

A third number is the **step**: `word[1:7:2]` takes every second character, and `word[::-1]` steps backwards through the whole thing, which is how text gets reversed. Unlike indexing, a slice never raises for being out of range - it hands back whatever is actually there, which may be nothing at all.
sections.code:
word = "grimoire"
print(word[0:4])
print(word[4:])
print(word[:4])
print(word[-3:])
print(word[1:7:2])
print(word[10:14] + "(nothing)")

annotations.text: Characters 0, 1, 2 and 3 - four of them, because 4 - 0 = 4. Index 4 is excluded, which is why the next line can start at 4 without repeating anything.
Start 1, stop before 7, step 2: indexes 1, 3 and 5. The step counts from the start index, not from zero.
Both ends lie past the end of the word, so the slice is empty. Compare word[10], which would raise IndexError - slicing forgives where indexing refuses.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill the two blanks so the program prints `moir`.
checkpoint.explain: `m` sits at index 3 and `r` at index 6, so the stop must be 7 - one past the last character wanted. Writing 6 is the commonest slip, and it silently gives `moi` rather than raising, which is why half-open intervals have to be understood rather than guessed at.

sections.title: Methods, and the String You Cannot Edit
sections.body:
A **method** is a function that belongs to a value and is called by writing a dot after it, as in `title.upper()`. Text comes with a large set of them, and a handful cover most real work: `strip` removes blank space from both ends, `lower` and `upper` change case, `replace` swaps one run of characters for another, `startswith` and `endswith` answer True or False, and `find` reports the index where something begins, or `-1` when it is not there at all.

Every one of those methods **returns a new piece of text and leaves the original exactly as it was**. Writing `title.strip()` on a line by itself accomplishes nothing: the cleaned-up text is built, nobody catches it, and it is thrown away. You have to keep the result with `title = title.strip()`, or use it on the spot.

The reason is that strings are **immutable** - once made, the characters inside one can never change. So `title[0] = "T"` is not a slow way of doing it or a matter of style, it is impossible, and Python says so with `TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment`.

That sounds like a restriction and mostly is not. It means text handed to a function cannot be altered behind the caller's back, and it is why methods chain safely: each one gives the next a fresh result instead of everybody scribbling on one shared value. To change a character, build a new string around it, as in `title[:1].upper() + title[1:]`.
sections.code:
title = "  the Serpent's Ascent  "
print(title.strip())
print(title.strip().upper())
print(title.strip().replace("Serpent", "Dragon"))
print(title.strip().startswith("the"))
print(title.strip().find("Ascent"))
print(len(title))

annotations.text: Chaining reads left to right: strip runs first and hands its new string to upper. Neither one touches the value that title names.
find returns an index, and returns -1 rather than raising when the text is absent. -1 is itself a real index of a real character, so never use the answer without checking it.
Still 24. Five methods were called on it and title is untouched, because none of them could have touched it.

checkpoint.explain: The tempting answer is `QUIET` twice, from reading line 2 as an instruction that changes `s`. It is not one: it builds an uppercase string, hands it to nobody, and the value is discarded. Only the expression whose result gets used - line 4 - shows any effect.

sections.title: Taking Text Apart, and Building It Back
sections.body:
`split` cuts text into its parts at a separator you name, and hands back a **list** - a numbered sequence of values, which has a whole floor of its own later; for now it is enough that `len` counts it and square brackets index it exactly as they do text. `line.split(",")` turns `"a,b,c"` into three separate pieces. Called with no separator at all, `split()` cuts on blank space and quietly ignores runs of it, which is nearly always what is wanted for breaking a sentence into words.

`join` is the exact reverse, and its shape surprises people: you call it on the **separator** and hand it the parts. `" - ".join(runes)` glues the parts back together with ` - ` between them. It reads backwards until you notice that the separator is the thing that knows how to do the gluing.

To build a line out of values you already hold, put an `f` before the opening quote and write the values in braces: `f"{count} runes"`. Any expression fits inside the braces and the result is an ordinary new string. Stitching pieces together with `+` instead forces you to convert every number by hand and buries the shape of the line in punctuation.

Cut apart, transform, put back is one of the most useful shapes in the language, and it is worth recognising as a shape rather than as three separate tricks.
sections.code:
line = "algiz,ehwaz,laguz"
runes = line.split(",")
print(runes)
print(runes[1])
print(" - ".join(runes))
print("algiz  ehwaz   laguz".split())
count = len(runes)
print(f"{count} runes, first is {runes[0]}")

annotations.text: The parts print inside square brackets with quotes round each one - that is a list being shown, not a piece of text.
split() with no argument collapses the runs of spaces, so three words come back rather than a scattering of empty pieces.
count is a number and the f-string converts it for you. Writing count + " runes" instead would raise TypeError.

checkpoint.prompt: Write `dashed(text)` which returns the words of `text` in upper case, joined with single hyphens. `dashed("one two")` is `"ONE-TWO"`, and runs of spaces between words must not produce empty pieces.
checkpoint.explain: Cutting on the space character with `split(" ")` passes the first test and fails the second, because a run of three spaces becomes two empty pieces between the words. The no-argument form exists precisely for this, and the second test is there to catch the version that does not use it.

guided-practice.explain: Two characters added together make a two-character string, not a sum - `+` between pieces of text joins them. The second line is the one that catches people: index 2 is the third character, because the counting started at zero.
guided-practice.hint: Write the indexes above the letters: a is 0, n is 1, s is 2, u is 3, z is 4. Then read off what each expression asks for.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so the program prints `cant` on the first line and `ation` on the second.
guided-practice.explain: The same number 6 does two different jobs here: as a stop it is one past the last character taken, and as a start it is the first character taken. That is the half-open interval in a single program - the two slices meet at 6 and neither drop nor repeat a character.
guided-practice.hint: Number the letters from zero: i0 n1 c2 a3 n4 t5 a6 t7 i8 o9 n10. Remember the stop index is excluded.

guided-practice.code:
motto = "Speak Softly"
motto.lower()
print(motto)
print(motto.lower())
print(motto.replace(" ", ""))
print(motto)
guided-practice.answer:
Speak Softly
speak softly
SpeakSoftly
Speak Softly
guided-practice.explain: Line 2 and line 5 both build new strings that nothing keeps, so `motto` is identical on the first and last lines of output. The tempting reading is that a method call is a command that modifies the value; it is an expression that produces one.
guided-practice.hint: Ask of every method call: was the result stored anywhere, or used anywhere? If not, it changed nothing.

guided-practice.prompt: `capitalise_first(word)` should return the word with its first character in upper case and the rest untouched, and should return empty text unchanged. It raises `TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment`. Repair it.
guided-practice.explain: No repair keeps the shape of the broken line, because assigning into a string is not something Python can do at all - the fix has to build a new string. Note that `word[0].upper() + word[1:]` passes three of the four tests and raises IndexError on the empty one; a one-character slice is empty rather than an error, which is what makes `word[:1]` the safer half of the pair.
guided-practice.hint: You cannot change a character in place. Build the answer out of two pieces and add them together - and pick a first piece that survives an empty word.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `ends(text)` returning the first and last characters of `text` stuck together. `ends("grimoire")` is `"ge"`. Text of one character returns that character, and empty text returns empty text.
guided-practice.explain: `text[-1]` is the whole reason this stays short: without it you would write `text[len(text) - 1]` and get the minus one wrong sooner or later. The empty test is not decoration - `text[0]` on empty text raises IndexError, so the guard has to come before the indexing rather than after it.
guided-practice.hint: `text[-1]` is the last character whatever the length. The one-character case needs its own answer, because otherwise the first and last character are the same one and it would appear twice.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `mirror(text)` returning `text` followed immediately by the same text backwards. `mirror("ab")` is `"abba"`. Reverse it with a slice that has a step, not with a loop.
guided-practice.explain: `text[::-1]` leaves both ends blank and sets the step to -1, so it runs the whole thing backwards. `text[-1:0:-1]` is the near miss: it stops before index 0 and silently loses the first character, which the empty and one-character tests would not catch but `grim` does.
guided-practice.hint: Leave the start and the stop of the slice empty and give it a step of -1.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `tidy(name)` which returns `name` with blank space removed from both ends, put into lower case, and with every hyphen turned into a single space. `tidy("  Ada-Lovelace ")` is `"ada lovelace"`. Chain the string methods rather than writing a loop.
guided-practice.explain: The chain works because each method returns a new string for the next one to act on - nothing is modified along the way. The version that calls the three methods on separate lines without assigning anything looks almost identical and returns the original name untouched, which is the mistake this floor exists to make unmissable.
guided-practice.hint: Three method calls in a row on one line: strip, then lower, then replace. `replace` takes what to look for first and what to put there second.

guided-practice.prompt: Write `summarise(csv_line)` which takes text holding pieces separated by commas and returns a summary line built with an f-string: the number of pieces, then ` items: `, then the pieces rejoined with ` | ` between them. `summarise("a,b,c")` is `"3 items: a | b | c"`.
guided-practice.explain: The last test is the surprising one: cutting empty text at commas gives one piece, and that piece is empty, so the count is 1 rather than 0. Splitting never yields nothing - if the separator is absent you get the whole text back as a single piece, which is what the `solo` case shows.
guided-practice.hint: Put the whole join expression inside the braces of the f-string. Use single quotes for the separator inside the braces so they do not close the double-quoted f-string.

independent-practice.prompt: Write `initials(full_name)`. Given somebody's full name, return their initials: the first letter of each word in upper case, separated by full stops, with no full stop after the last one. `initials("ada byron lovelace")` is `"A.B.L"`. Extra blank space anywhere in the name must not produce empty initials, and a name with no words at all returns empty text.
independent-practice.explain: The separator goes between the initials, never after the last one, so adding a full stop each time round and trimming the end afterwards is the fiddly route. Adding the separator only when there is already something to separate from needs no cleanup at all, and it is the same reasoning that makes gluing pieces back together the natural fit here.

independent-practice.prompt: Write `redact(text, secret)`. Every appearance of `secret` inside `text` must come back replaced by a row of asterisks of the same length, so the line keeps its width. `redact("my code is 1234", "1234")` is `"my code is ****"`. If the secret does not appear, the text comes back unchanged.
independent-practice.solution:
def redact(text, secret):
    return text.replace(secret, "*" * len(secret))
independent-practice.explain: The third test rules out finding the secret once and rebuilding round that position - every appearance has to go, and there are three of them. `"*" * len(secret)` is repetition of text by a number, which is what keeps the replacement the original width instead of collapsing it to a single star.

independent-practice.prompt: Write `is_palindrome(text)` returning `True` when `text` reads the same forwards and backwards once spaces are ignored and case is disregarded, and `False` otherwise. `is_palindrome("Never odd or even")` is `True`. Text with nothing in it counts as a palindrome.

tests.input: 'Was it a car or a cat I saw'

independent-practice.explain: Cleaning first and comparing once is far less error-prone than walking two positions towards each other, because the walking version has to skip spaces on both sides at the same time and its stopping condition is easy to get wrong. Comparing the cleaned text with its own reverse is a single expression with no boundary left to misjudge.

independent-practice.prompt: Write `field(line, n)`. `line` holds pieces separated by commas, and `n` says which piece is wanted, counting the first as 0. Return that piece with any blank space at its ends removed. If `n` names a piece that is not there - including a negative `n` - return empty text. `field("a, b ,c", 1)` is `"b"`.
independent-practice.explain: The negative test is the trap. Python is perfectly happy with position -1 and would hand back the last piece, so the guard has to reject negatives explicitly - a check that only asks whether `n` is too large passes three tests and quietly returns the wrong answer on the fourth.

independent-practice.prompt: Write `title_line(heading)` returning `heading` with blank space at the ends removed, each word's first letter in upper case and the rest of each word in lower case, and exactly one space between words. `title_line("  the SERPENT's ascent ")` is `"The Serpent's Ascent"`.
independent-practice.explain: Python has a built-in `title` method and it fails the first test, returning `The Serpent'S Ascent` - it treats the apostrophe as a word boundary and raises the letter after it. That is why the first test carries an apostrophe: the shortest answer here is the wrong one, and only a test that knows where it breaks will say so.

independent-practice.prompt: Write `describe(word)` returning a single line of exactly this shape: `grimoire has 8 letters, from g to e`. The number is the letter count, and the two single letters are the first and the last of the word. If the word is empty, return `empty` instead.

tests.expected: grimoire has 8 letters, from g to e
x has 1 letters, from x to x
ab has 2 letters, from a to b

independent-practice.explain: Building this line by adding pieces together fails on the count, because a number cannot be added to text - it would need converting by hand at exactly the point where the line is already hardest to read. The one-letter test also shows why the empty case needs a branch of its own rather than a clever slice: with no letters there is no first and no last to name.

exam.prompt: A Python string is **immutable**. Which of these is what that word means?
choices: Its characters cannot be read once it has been created.
No operation can alter the characters of an existing string; anything that looks like a change produces a new string instead.
It cannot be stored under more than one name at a time.
It can hold letters but never digits or punctuation.
exam.explain: Immutability is about writing, not reading, and the first option confuses the two. The point is that every method appears to change the text and in fact returns a fresh one, which is why forgetting to keep the result is such a common and silent bug.

exam.prompt: In the slice `text[2:5]`, which positions of `text` end up in the result?
exam.explain: The stop is excluded, so the result holds 5 - 2 = 3 characters. The second option is the intuitive guess from everyday language, where 'two to five' includes five, and it is why so many slices come out one character too long on the first attempt.

The last line is the one worth pausing on: `word[7]` would raise IndexError, but the slice `word[7:9]` is simply empty, so adding `end` to it prints `end` on its own. Slicing forgives out-of-range positions; indexing does not.

exam.code:
raw = "north::south::east"
parts = raw.split("::")
print(parts)
print(len(parts))
print("/".join(parts))
print("-".join("ab"))
exam.explain: A separator can be longer than one character, so `::` cuts at each pair rather than at each colon - cutting on a single colon would give five pieces, two of them empty. The last line catches most people: gluing a piece of text walks its characters, so `ab` becomes `a-b`.

exam.prompt: Fill the three blanks with method names so the program prints `rune stone`.
exam.explain: Each method hands its new string to the next, which is only possible because none of them modifies `raw`. The order of the first two does not matter here, but the two arguments to the last one do: `replace` takes what to look for first and what to put in its place second.

exam.prompt: Put these lines in order to make a working `last_word(sentence)` that returns the final word of a sentence in upper case, and empty text when there are no words.
exam.explain: The guard has to sit after the cutting and before the indexing, because it is the cut-up result that might be empty and the indexing that would fail on it. Putting the guard first would test the sentence rather than the words, and a sentence of nothing but spaces would slip past it straight into an IndexError.

exam.prompt: A colleague's function begins with the line `name.strip()` and they cannot work out why the leading spaces are still there afterwards. Explain what that line actually does, what becomes of its result, and what they should have written instead.
exam.explain: The line is not wrong so much as pointless: it builds the stripped text correctly and then throws it away, because nothing catches the result. This is the everyday consequence of immutability - `name = name.strip()` is the fix, and the same shape applies to every method on this floor.

exam.prompt: Write `slugify(title)` returning `title` in lower case with the blank space at its ends removed and every run of spaces between words turned into a single hyphen. `slugify("  The Serpent's Ascent ")` is `"the-serpent's-ascent"`.
exam.explain: Replacing every space with a hyphen passes the first two tests and fails the third, turning a run of three spaces into three hyphens. Cutting the text into words and gluing them back gets runs of space right for free, because the cutting has already discarded them.

exam.prompt: Write `initial_and_surname(full_name)` returning a name in the shape `A. Lovelace` - the first word reduced to its opening letter in upper case followed by a full stop and a space, then the last word with its first letter in upper case and the rest of it unchanged. A single word comes back with just its first letter raised, and a name with no words at all returns empty text.
exam.explain: The middle name in the second test is the point: taking the second word rather than the last one passes the first test and fails this one. Position -1 says what is actually meant - the final word - without needing to know how many words there are.
